newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Embattled Kazakh government to overhaul pensions.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Kazakh government to overhaul pensions.

text.p: Kazakhstan's government, anxious about growing impatience with unpaid wages and pensions, is planning to launch a new national pension scheme using private funds.
"I am not going to conceal the fact that our State Pension Fund has gone bankrupt," Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Pavlov told a news conference on Thursday.
The new pension scheme appeared to be the government's most serious attempt yet to ease social tensions and boost people's confidence in economic reform.
Pensioners have been hardest hit by the government's efforts to turn round the unwieldy and energy-guzzling economy.
President Nursultan Nazarbayev has threatened to sack his prime minister if he does not redress the situation by April 10.
The government owes pensioners 34 billion tenge ($450 million). Pavlov said the pension scheme inherited from Soviet days "has practically exhausted its potential".
The government could tap international capital markets to help pay for setting up the new scheme, Pavlov said.
In Soviet times, all enterprises and institutions were obliged to make monthly payments to a single state pension fund from the salaries of each employee.

But Grigory Marchenko, chairman of the National Securities Commission, said the economic crisis meant many Kazakh companies now viewed payments to the pension fund as another kind of tax and were "enthusiastically avoiding it".

The demographic situation in the fast-ageing Central Asian state of 16.9 million people has also changed since the beginning of the 1990s, when five workers funded one pensioner. Now the proportion is 1.8 workers per pensioner.
Marchenko told the news conference the government was now planning to create a system of national private pension funds to be funded by employee pension payments.
New western-style management funds would manage the assets, investing in Kazakshstan's nascent debt and stock markets.
However, establishing the private pension funds will take up to 30 years, Marchenko said, with the role of the State Pension Fund to be reduced to zero within 10 years.
